title: At the café and the market
topic: ordering politely; prices; numbers from 11 to 100
why: Ordering at a café, asking a price at the market and counting up to 100: everything you need to get by in the most common situations in Israel. The lesson reuses the present of רוֹצֶה and the numbers from 0 to 10.

{"lessons": ["

Ordering politely

In Israel, people order very directly: אֲנִי רוֹצֶה… (a man) or אֲנִי רוֹצָה… (a woman), \"I want.\" With בְּבַקָּשָׁה (please), it's perfectly polite: no need for \"I'd like\" or \"could I have.\"

אֲנִי רוֹצָה קָפֶה הָפוּךְ, בְּבַקָּשָׁה.I'd like a latte, please. [ani rotsa kafe hafukh, bevakasha]

Another very common phrase: אֶפְשָׁר…? (\"is it possible?\") followed by what you want. It never changes, for men and women alike.

אֶפְשָׁר כּוֹס מַיִם?Can I have a glass of water? [efshar kos mayim?]

The waiter asks עוֹד מַשֶּׁהוּ? (anything else?). You answer זֶה הַכֹּל, תּוֹדָה (that's all, thanks).

קָפֶה הָפוּךְ, literally \"upside-down coffee,\" is the frothy milky coffee, a kind of latte, that people drink all over Israel.

", "

Numbers from 11 to 100

From 11 to 19: the unit, slightly shortened, then עֶשְׂרֵה (esre), a bit like \"-teen\" in English. The tens end in ־ִים, like a plural: עֶשְׂרִים (20) comes from עֶשֶׂר (10).

For 21, 35, 42…, the tens come first, as in English, but joined with \"and\": \"twenty and one.\" עֶשְׂרִים וְאַחַת (21), שְׁלוֹשִׁים וְחָמֵשׁ (35), אַרְבָּעִים וּשְׁתַּיִם (42: before a shva, וְ becomes וּ, \"u\").

These are the counting forms, like 0 to 10. They're also used for age, with בֶּן as well as with בַּת: הוּא בֶּן עֶשְׂרִים וְאַחַת, הִיא בַּת עֶשְׂרִים וְאַחַת (he / she is 21).

", "

At the market: how much is it?

At the שׁוּק (shuk, the market), the key question: כַּמָּה זֶה עוֹלֶה? (how much is it?). You can also name the product: כַּמָּה עוֹלֶה קִילוֹ עַגְבָנִיּוֹת? (how much is a kilo of tomatoes?).

The currency is the שֶׁקֶל (shekel), plural שְׁקָלִים (shkalim), symbol ₪. In speech, after a number, Israelis often keep the singular:

זֶה עוֹלֶה עֶשְׂרִים שֶׁקֶל.It costs twenty shekels. [ze ole esrim shekel]

To react: יָקָר! (that's expensive!) or זוֹל! (cheap!). The adjective agrees: הַתַּפּוּחַ יָקָר (the apple is expensive), הָעוּגָה יְקָרָה (the cake is expensive): in Hebrew, apple is masculine and cake is feminine, so learn the gender with each noun!

No \"of\" between the quantity and the product: קִילוֹ עַגְבָנִיּוֹת, literally \"a kilo tomatoes.\"
